changes.text: - Newmark Permanent-Displacement Formulations

changes.source: Diana Appendix E wording restored from deleted content
changes.text: The seismic-coefficient section applies five Newmark permanent-displacement formulations: three rigid-block models, two flexible-block models and, among the latter, the BM branch selected by the tectonic control of the project. This section reproduces the published form of each formulation, including both BM branches, and states the rule that defines the active configuration. The rigid-block formulations relate the displacement to measures of the base excitation, whereas the flexible-block formulations additionally incorporate the dynamic response of the sliding mass through its fundamental period Ts and the spectral acceleration evaluated at a period proportional to Ts.

changes.text: This section reports the dynamic properties of the slopes analyzed, the permanent displacements induced by the design earthquakes accumulate in their potential sliding masses, and the performance-based seismic coefficients derived from those displacements. The flexible sliding-block displacement models require the fundamental period of each potential sliding mass and the dynamic soil stiffness that determines it: the analyses considered 5 geometry–material scenarios with heights between 27 and 135 m, and the estimated fundamental period varies between 0.22 and 1.28 s.

changes.text: Slope Performance under the design earthquakes is evaluated through successive tiers of analysis including pseudostatic stability checks, simplified estimates of permanent deformation, and dynamic analyses where warranted by the consequences of failure, anticipated response, or complexity of the failure mechanism (International Commission on Large Dams, 2016; Federal Emergency Management Agency, 2005). Within this framework, the Newmark method provides a deformation-based assessment that complements the limit-equilibrium analysis. The pseudostatic seismic coefficient is a project-specific value rather than assigned as a universal value for a particular structure type. USACE manuals EM 1110-2-1902 and EM 1110-2-2100 discuss pseudostatic analysis  sliding block methods for evaluating seismic stability and permanent deformation Selection of the coefficient considers the site-specific seismic hazard, potential failure mechanism, and  project performance criteria (U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, 2003; U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, 2005).

changes.text: The allowable permanent displacement is expressed as a percentage of the reference slope height.  This report evaluates four relative displacement thresholds, Da/H = 0.1, 0.4, 1.0, 2.5%, based on the crest-settlement ratios  reported by Alberti et. al. (Aliberti, Biondi, Cascone, & Rampello, 2019).  The reference height includes the embankment height and the thickness of the deformable foundation and is adopted here as the slope height for normalization. The seismic coefficient tables are presented for these four thresholds. Section 10.1.3 describes the derivation of the coefficients from the allowable displacement.

changes.text: Seismic (Pseudo-Static) Coefficients

changes.source: chapter 10 saved equation and cross-reference labels retained; duplicate identical citation displays removed
changes.text: Pseudostatic seismic design of slopes requires a horizontal coefficient representing earthquake loading on the sliding mass. In this section the coefficient is derived from displacement-based performance: the Newmark permanent displacement Dn is the slope-deformation performance measure, and the coefficient kmax is the lowest yield coefficient ky consistent with a performance objective defined by the allowable displacement Da and the target maximum exceedance probability pe,  such that Dn exceeds Da. The normalized coefficient kh expresses kmax as a percentage of the site-adjusted PGA expressed in units of (g) after site response is accounted for in each geometry–material combination, and the coefficients are reported by geometry, material and seismic demand. For the slopes considered, Dn is estimated probabilistically by combining empirical regression models within a lognormal framework.

changes.source: chapter 10 saved equation and cross-reference labels retained; duplicate identical citation displays removed
changes.text: The horizontal pseudostatic coefficient is derived in this assessment from the allowable permanent displacement Da of the potentially sliding mass (Bray & Travasarou, Pseudostatic Coefficient for Use in Simplified Seismic Slope Stability Evaluation, 2009; Macedo, Bray, Abrahamson, & Travasarou, 2018). The seismic demand and the fundamental periods established in the preceding sections allow the Dn(ky) relations between the Newmark permanent displacement and the yield coefficient to be computed; their inversion at the target exceedance probability yields kmax, and its normalization by the PGA transformed to the VS30 of each geometry–material combination yields kh, so that the result traceably links the deformation objective to the horizontal action employed in the stability verification. The yield acceleration ay represents the acceleration level at which the limit-equilibrium factor of safety equals unity and its dimensionless form is ky=ay/g; for each allowable displacement and target exceedance probability, the analysis determines the minimum ky threshold that satisfies the performance criterion, and that threshold is kmax, the coefficient applied in the pseudostatic limit-equilibrium verification. A factor of safety of at least unity under this applied coefficient indicates that the calculated yield coefficient meets or exceeds the required threshold.

changes.source: chapter 10 saved equation and cross-reference labels retained; duplicate identical citation displays removed
changes.text: In the Newmark sliding-block method (Newmark, 1965), the potentially sliding wedge is represented as a rigid block resting on an inclined plane: relative motion begins when the driving acceleration exceeds the yield acceleration ay=kyg and continues until the relative velocity returns to zero, and the permanent displacement is the sum of those episodes over the duration of the earthquake motion, obtained by double integration of the acceleration excess. The extension of the procedure to dams and embankments (Makdisi & Seed, 1978) derived the equivalent acceleration of the sliding mass from its dynamic response and is the direct antecedent of the flexible formulations. The adopted empirical relations represent the accumulated displacement statistically through two idealizations: rigid-block models relate the displacement to measures of the base excitation, and flexible-block models additionally incorporate the dynamic response of the mass through Ts and the spectral acceleration evaluated at a period proportional to Ts.

changes.source: chapter 10 saved equation and cross-reference labels retained; duplicate identical citation displays removed
changes.text: The displacement calculation uses the seismic demand and the fundamental periods established in Section 10.1.2. For each geometry, material and seismic demand – the probabilistic spectrum of each evaluated return period – a joint sample of the intensity measures required by the rigid-block and flexible formulations is constructed; that sample is common to all models, so their differences represent the displacement formulation rather than incompatible seismic demands. The input for each return period is the reference-rock UHS, which for 10,000 years represents the MDE; it specifies spectral acceleration ordinates at a common annual exceedance rate and is defined for VS30=Vref=760 m/s. For each geometry and material scenario, the spectral ordinates and the PGA are transformed to the corresponding VS30 through the ST20 amplification model (Stewart, et al., 2020; Hashash, Ilhan, & Harmon, 2020).

changes.source: chapter 10 saved equation and cross-reference labels retained; duplicate identical citation displays removed
changes.text: At the site condition of each scenario, the joint sample comprises PGA, Sa(1.3Ts), and Sa(1.5Ts). The three measures are represented through empirical marginals in ln(Sa) and a Gaussian copula with the full inter-period correlation matrix (Baker & Jayaram, 2008), and the samples are recentered to preserve the mean of each amplified marginal; in each realization, the three intensities remain paired, and each displacement formulation uses the measures entering its regression. The Arias intensity that JB07 and SR08 require completes the set of intensity measures; it is estimated deterministically for each realization from the PGA, so that each PGA realization determines a single value of IA and the displacement sample propagates the PGA variability.

changes.source: chapter 10 saved equation and cross-reference labels retained; duplicate identical citation displays removed
changes.text: For each scenario, 30 values of ky are evaluated, logarithmically spaced between 0.01 and max(PGA,0.80), where PGA is the mean site-condition PGA of the scenario; that interval establishes the computed range of the Dn(ky) relations, over which the formulations are evaluated and the inversion to kmax operates.

changes.source: chapter 10 saved equation and cross-reference labels retained; duplicate identical citation displays removed
changes.text: Each active formulation estimates the Newmark permanent displacement (Newmark, 1965) of the sliding mass from the yield acceleration and the intensity measures of its regression, and all of them express the positive displacement Dn, in centimeters, through

changes.source: chapter 10 saved equation and cross-reference labels retained; duplicate identical citation displays removed
changes.text: Dn=exp​μlnD+ϵσlnD,  ϵ∼N(0,1),[Eq. 1013]

changes.source: chapter 10 saved equation and cross-reference labels retained; duplicate identical citation displays removed
changes.text: where μlnD and σlnD are the mean and standard deviation of lnDn defined by each model, and ϵ is a standard-normal residual. Some source formulations contain a discrete branch of zero or negligible displacement; the implemented evaluation uses exclusively the positive lognormal branch, conditional on displacement exceeding the model’s zero-or-negligible-displacement threshold. In every formulation, ky, PGA, and Sa are expressed in units of g – the acceleration of gravity – IA in m/s, and Ts in seconds; the Arias intensity is derived from the PGA of each realization, and the reference magnitude is Mw= 5.5 for return periods up to 2,500 years and Mw= 6.5 for return periods of 5,000 and 10,000 years. Within each demand, that magnitude is common to the geometry, material and site combinations evaluated. The published form of each formulation is reproduced in Appendix E. The performance-based seismic coefficient is defined by

changes.text: kmax(pe∣Da)=infky:P[Dn(ky)>Da]≤pe.[Eq. 1014]

changes.source: chapter 10 saved equation and cross-reference labels retained; duplicate identical citation displays removed
changes.text: where pe is the target probability that Dn exceeds Da: kmax is the smallest ky for which the probability of exceeding the allowable displacement is at most pe. The normalized coefficient, reported as a percentage of the PGA [% of PGA], is calculated using the site-adjusted PGA transformed to the VS30 of the geometry–material combination evaluated for each demand:

changes.source: chapter 10 saved equation and cross-reference labels retained; duplicate identical citation displays removed

changes.source: chapter 10 saved equation and cross-reference labels retained; duplicate identical citation displays removed
changes.text: kmax is expressed in units of g and kh as a percentage of the PGA of the corresponding site condition. These two quantities express the displacement criterion as the horizontal action of the pseudostatic verification.

changes.source: chapter 10 saved equation and cross-reference labels retained; duplicate identical citation displays removed
changes.text: The five formulations are evaluated individually and combined into the three sets that the tables and figures identify as IDn: rigid, flexible and ensemble. The displacement model provides individual realizations for AM88, JB07, SR08, BT07, and a fifth formulation selected by the tectonic context: BM17 for projects with subduction control and BM19 for projects with shallow crustal control. The overall design set, identified as ensemble, combines AM88, JB07, SR08, BT07, and the active BM branch with equal weights; the rigid family combines AM88, JB07, and SR08, and the flexible family combines BT07 and the active BM branch. The rigid family thus relates the displacement to measures of the base excitation, the flexible family additionally incorporates the dynamic response of the sliding mass through Ts, and the ensemble is the design set that combines both. For each ky, the displacements of a family are summarized from the weighted empirical distribution of the realizations of its models.

changes.source: chapter 10 saved equation and cross-reference labels retained; duplicate identical citation displays removed
changes.text: All models receive the same joint sample of PGA and spectral accelerations, and a single realization of ϵ is shared across the models and across all values of ky; each formulation scales that residual through its own σlnD, and the sampled PGA is retained with each realization so that the inversion preserves the pairing between displacement and seismic demand. The realizations of Dn are calculated for each material class with its mean dynamic properties; the fractiles of the stiffness profiles and of Ts are not propagated as additional realizations in the displacement calculation, and each material class is kept as an separate scenario through the inversion to kmax, so the displacement curves are not averaged across materials before that operation.

changes.source: chapter 10 saved equation and cross-reference labels retained; duplicate identical citation displays removed
changes.text: For each model and realization, the computed Dn(ky) relation is projected onto a non-increasing curve and inverted in the (lnDn,lnky) plane to solve the criterion of Eq. 1014; when Da falls outside the calculated range, the relation is extrapolated in that plane from the two points at the corresponding end, with the single exception of the AM88 limit treated in Appendix E. The inversion is performed first for each model within each realization.

changes.source: chapter 10 saved equation and cross-reference labels retained; duplicate identical citation displays removed
changes.text: The root distributions of the models are then combined with the family weights and summarized through the arithmetic mean and the empirical fractiles q=0.05, 0.10, 0.16, 0.50, 0.84, 0.90, and 0.95 (Verri Kozlowski, 2026). Because of the decreasing relation between Dn and ky, the fractile associated with the exceedance target satisfies Eq. 1016, where q=0.84 corresponds to an exceedance probability of pe=16%.

changes.source: chapter 10 saved equation and cross-reference labels retained; duplicate identical citation displays removed
chapter 10 saved equation and cross-reference labels retained; duplicate identical citation displays removed
changes.text: The q fractiles are therefore the statistics associated with the criterion expressed through pe; the arithmetic mean summarizes the center of the simulated distribution and does not represent a target probability. The evaluation uses 300 realizations for each demand – the probabilistic spectrum of each return period TR = 475, 2,475, 10,000 years – and a grid of allowable displacements Da/Hs ranging from 0.05 to 2.50 %. This grid contains, for every slope height, the damage thresholds Da/H = 0.1, 0.4, 1.0, 2.5% of Section 10.1.1, at which the coefficient tables are reported; values of Da that exceed the calculated range of a realization are obtained through the logarithmic extrapolation defined above.
